executable.help:
Guffin - native GGUF chat on Metal

Usage: guffin -m MODEL [options]
       guffin inspect MODEL

Chat is the default. Give a prompt for one answer and exit.
Chat shows prompt/generation rates and internal TTFT after each reply.

  -m, --model FILE          Model GGUF (or use positional MODEL)
  -p, --prompt TEXT         Answer TEXT once, then exit
  -n, --max-new-tokens N    Optional reply token limit
  -c, --context-size N      Context capacity in tokens
      --draft-model FILE    Enable lossless speculative decoding
      --temperature T       Sampling temperature (default: 0.8)
      --greedy              Select the most likely token
      --seed N              Sampling seed (default: random)
      --stats               Also show timing for one-shot/piped output
  -h, --help                Show this help
      --help-all            Include advanced options
      --version             Show build identity

Examples:
  guffin -m models/gemma-3-12b-it-Q4_K_M.gguf
  guffin -m MODEL --draft-model DRAFT
  guffin -m MODEL -p "Explain unified memory" -n 128

turns.prompt: Could you write a captivating short story beginning with the sentence: The old abandoned house at the end of the street held a secret that no one had ever discovered.
turns.answer:
The old abandoned house at the end of the street held a secret that no one had ever discovered. It wasn’t the kind of secret whispered in gossip, or hinted at in local legend. It was a secret woven into the very fabric of the place, a silent hum vibrating within the rotting timbers and choked rose bushes. Locals called it Blackwood Manor, and children dared each other to run past, convinced it was haunted by the mournful sighs of its last resident, a reclusive inventor named Elias Blackwood.

I, however, wasn't afraid. I was fifteen, bored, and possessed of an insatiable curiosity. My name is Finn, and I was determined to unravel Blackwood’s mystery. Everyone said he'd gone mad, vanished without a trace, leaving behind a house filled with strange contraptions and unanswered questions. The police had searched, of course, but declared it a case of simple abandonment. I suspected otherwise.

For weeks, I’d watched the house, observing the patterns of the overgrown garden, the way the moonlight fell on the boarded-up windows. Finally, I found a loose board, pried it free, and slipped inside.

The air within was thick with dust and the scent of decay. Cobwebs clung to everything, shimmering like macabre lace. The house was a labyrinth of rooms, each cluttered with bizarre machinery: gears, wires, copper tubing, all connected by a network of intricate levers and dials. They looked like the insides of a giant, forgotten clockwork beast.

I explored, my heart pounding a nervous rhythm against my ribs.  In the library, I found notebooks filled with Elias Blackwood’s frantic handwriting, sketches of fantastical devices, and rambling philosophical musings on time and perception. He wrote of “bending the river of moments,” of “capturing the echoes of what might be.”

Then, in the basement, I found it. A single, circular room, bathed in an eerie, pulsing green light. In the center stood a device unlike anything I had ever seen. It resembled a massive brass telescope, but instead of a lens, it had a complex array of crystals that shimmered with the same unsettling green glow. 

As I approached, the air grew heavy, buzzing with energy. I reached out, hesitantly, and touched a crystal.

The world dissolved. 

Not violently, but gradually, like a watercolor painting being washed away by rain. I wasn’t in the basement anymore. I was in the garden, but the roses were blooming in colours I’d never seen – silver, gold, and a vibrant, pulsing violet. A young woman, laughing, watered the flowers. She looked exactly like the faded photograph I'd seen of Elias Blackwood’s wife. 

Then she turned, and her eyes met mine. They weren’t the eyes of a woman from the past. They were filled with a profound sadness and a desperate plea. 

"He trapped them," she whispered, her voice echoing in my mind. "He trapped all the moments, all the possibilities. He wanted to hold onto time, but he only created a prison."

Suddenly, the vision flickered, threatened to disappear. I stumbled back, withdrawing my hand from the crystal. The basement returned, the green light dimming. 

I understood now. Elias Blackwood hadn’t gone mad. He'd been trying to build a machine to capture time, to relive cherished moments. But he’d inadvertently created a pocket dimension, a repository of alternate realities, and trapped the people who lived within them. 

I knew I couldn't leave them. But I also knew I couldn’t free them alone.  I carefully replaced the loose board, a new sense of purpose burning within me. The secret of Blackwood Manor wasn’t about a mad inventor. It was about a desperate love, a flawed genius, and a prison of shimmering, stolen moments. 

And I, Finn, the bored teenager from the end of the street, was the only one who knew. And I knew I had a very big problem to solve.

The old house hid secrets. No one ever found them. Locals called it Blackwood Manor. Children dared to run past. They feared mournful sighs. I wasn't really scared. I felt intensely curious. My name is Finn. I wanted answers. Everyone said he vanished. He left strange machines. I suspected something else.

I watched the old house. I noted garden patterns. Moonlight hit boarded windows. I found a loose board. I slipped quietly inside. Dust choked the air. Decay filled every space. Cobwebs clung everywhere. Rooms formed a maze. Gears spun everywhere. Wires tangled wildly. They looked like beasts.

I explored every room. My heart beat fast. I found notebooks there. He wrote of time bending. He sketched strange devices. He pondered what might be. Then, the basement appeared. A room pulsed green light. A device stood central. Brass, crystals shimmered bright. 

I touched a crystal. The world faded slowly. I stood in the garden. Roses bloomed silver, gold. A woman laughed gently. She looked like his wife. She turned, met my gaze. Her eyes held deep sadness. "He trapped them all," she whispered. "He stole moments' echoes."

The vision flickered quickly. I stumbled backward fast. The basement returned dimly. He sought time's embrace. He built a prison then. Alternate realities shimmered. He trapped the living souls. I could not leave them. I couldn’t free them solo.

I replaced the loose board. New purpose burned brightly. The secret felt immense. It wasn’t inventor madness. It was love’s desperate plea. I knew one thing now. I had a big problem.
